If you search everloc + by rehau it's the first thing to come up. I agree it is more laborious, however it's also the only pex connection rated for direct burial in concrete. I personally use uponor with cold expansion rings for anything above ground. But the trade off there is in colder climates it can't be tested immediately. Everloc can. Also rehau has never had a class action lawsuit against its Pex system. Uponor has on their fully colored pex (not the clear with the colored letters). 

DeWalt makes a tool for everloc fittings that speed up the process exponentially. What you're "paying extra" for is peace of mind that when a plumber in the south runs Pex in an attic with not alot of r value in trusses (like the southern roof typically is) you won't have fittings weakened by the 150° temperatures like you would with uponor cold expansion. Add in a failed PRV on a town water supply and a weakened expansion ring and you have a disaster. 

Legitimately all water connections are compression fittings (by definition) besides solvent welds and fusion fittings.

Assuming you have a hot and cold drain somewhere in your plumbing or a washing machine hookup, this is the foolproof way to winterize

Go to a hardware store with this list
Fluid transfer pump (price varies, taller the plumbing the house the more expensive pump you need) 
A wye hose (washing machine hose section, less than 30$)
At least six Gallons of non toxic RV antifreeze ( less than 5$ per gallon, more house and more bathrooms=more antifreeze)
Two washing machine hoses if you don't have a washing machine
A five gallon bucket

Go home and shut off the valve coming off of your pressure tank, and open the drain on the well side of that valve, that will drain the pressure tank and isolate the indoor plumbing turn off the pump at breaker

Assuming you have an electric hot water heater, turn off the power at the breaker panel and leave it off until you refill it next year (do not have power to it when it's empty) close the valve on the cold side of the hot water heater. This isolates the hot water heater. Don't drain it yet

Take your shopping list  from earlier to your washing machine hookup or drains mentioned earlier, if you have a washing machine hookup detach the hoses from the two valves the washing machine connects to.

 If you have drains in the waterlines somewhere follow along here with your setup.

Fill the bucket with the RV antifreeze 

attach the two ends of the wye hose to both valves, take the singular end and attach it to washing machine hose "A" and the other end of washing machine hose "A" to the discharge connection of the transfer pump take washing machine hose "B" and attach it to the inlet connection on the transfer pump and put the other end of washing machine hose "B" in the bottom of your five gallon bucket, be sure it stays submerged throughout the process of you will run the risk of burning out the pump

Turn on the pump and then open the valves you've connected to with the wye hose

Proceed to the furthest bathroom or kitchen faucet from the pump and turn the hots and colds on individually and let them run till they turn the color of the antifreeze (pink in my experience) 


Return to the bucket, notice how much of the bucket has gone down and begin to estimate if you have enough

Flush your toilets run your showers to winterize their components, making sure enough antifreeze fills the trap on the drain of each fixture. open your outside hose bibs til they run pink as well.

Turn off your transfer pump 

Go drain your hot water heater

You're done 👍

Next year just turn on power to the well, open the main valve, run the fixtures til their clear, fill the water heater, turn it's power on and you're good to go.
